lines.en: Hi Omar! You said you had a strange week. What happened?
Hi Sara. I read the same news story in three languages, and not until then did I see how much of the news is framing.
What a headline chooses to shout and what it chooses to whisper tell you more than the story itself.
One channel called the protest 'unrest', another called it 'a movement'. Were the same event reported by two rival channels, you would hardly know it was the same event.
It is not only what the news reports that shapes opinion, but what it quietly leaves out.
And what the algorithm shows you is not the world; it is the world most likely to keep you watching.
This is why I started reading science news instead. At least scientists admit doubt.
What separates science from opinion is the willingness to say 'we do not know yet'.
It is a strength, not a weakness, that every scientific claim carries its own margin of doubt.
However elegant a theory may be, nature has no obligation to be elegant.
Speaking of big ideas, I have been reading philosophy again.
What makes a question philosophical is not that it has no answer, but that every answer opens ten more.
It is one thing to know the price of everything, and quite another to know the value of anything.
Not until we face the possibility that we are wrong do we truly begin to think.
It is argued that we do not see the world as it is, but as we are.
That would explain my uncle. But some questions are not philosophical at all, just human.
Like?
Like my friend who lost his father. Rarely does advice comfort the grieving; presence comforts them far more than words.
What empathy requires is not that we feel the same pain, but that we believe it is real.
Not until someone has sat with us in silence, without advice, do we feel truly heard.
It is said that courage is not the absence of fear, but the decision that something else matters more.
He told me he feels split between two countries, even though he has never left this one.
What we call 'normal' is usually nothing more than the habits of the people we grew up around.
However global the world becomes, people still dream in the language of their childhood.
Not until you live abroad do you discover which parts of you are you, and which are your country.
What the immigrant packs last and never unpacks is a way of being polite.
That might be the most beautiful sentence we have learned.
Little do we know of the storms inside the people we pass every day.
So, after your week of news and philosophy and grief, what did you conclude?
That the camera never lies, but it certainly chooses where to look. And so do we.
